body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The double diffusion method allows for disease identification and diagnosis and is an application of ...

A. Agglutination
B. Precipitation
C. Immunoassay
D. Fluorescent antibody test
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Agglutination | **F** | Agglutination involves particulate antigens. |
| B. Precipitation | **T** | Soluble antigen and antibody form precipitin lines in gel. |
| C. Immunoassay | **F** | Labelled immunoassays (ELISA, RIA) use tags; double diffusion is an unlabelled precipitation method. |
| D. Fluorescent antibody test | **F** | Uses fluorochrome-labelled antibodies. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Ouchterlony double diffusion**: antigen and antibody diffuse from separate wells in agar and form **precipitin lines** where they meet at equivalence. Line patterns show identity, partial identity or non-identity (used e.g. for fungal, ENA antibodies).

## Simplified explanation

Double diffusion is a precipitation test: soluble antigen and antibody meet in gel and form a visible line.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The ability of a single cytokine to alter the expression of several genes is called ...

A. Redundancy
B. Pleiotropy.
C. Autocrine stimulation
D. Endocrine effect.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Redundancy | **F** | Several cytokines having the same effect. |
| B. Pleiotropy. | **T** | One cytokine, many effects. |
| C. Autocrine stimulation | **F** | A cytokine acting on the cell that produced it. |
| D. Endocrine effect. | **F** | Action at a distant site via the circulation. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cytokine properties: **pleiotropy** (one cytokine, multiple actions/targets), **redundancy** (different cytokines, same effect), **synergy**, **antagonism**, **cascade induction**; modes of action: autocrine, paracrine, endocrine.

## Simplified explanation

Pleiotropy means one cytokine does many things.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is/are also known as the T-cell growth factor

A. IFN-γ
B. IL-12
C. IL-2
D. IL-10
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IFN-γ | **F** | Macrophage-activating cytokine (Th1). |
| B. IL-12 | **F** | Drives Th1 differentiation. |
| C. IL-2 | **T** | Originally named T-cell growth factor. |
| D. IL-10 | **F** | Anti-inflammatory/regulatory cytokine. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**IL-2** (T-cell growth factor), produced by activated CD4⁺ T cells, drives clonal expansion of T cells via the IL-2 receptor (CD25 = α chain) and supports Treg survival. Ciclosporin/tacrolimus block IL-2 transcription.

## Simplified explanation

IL-2 is the T-cell growth factor.
hint: Think of what activated T cells secrete to multiply.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The chemokine receptor(s) needed for cell specific binding in HIV is/are ...

A. CCR1
B. CCDR3
C. CCR4
D. CCR5
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. CCR1 | **F** | Not an HIV co-receptor. |
| B. CCDR3 | **F** | Not a recognised receptor name. |
| C. CCR4 | **F** | Not an HIV co-receptor. |
| D. CCR5 | **T** | Main co-receptor for macrophage-tropic (R5) HIV. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

HIV entry needs **CD4** plus a chemokine co-receptor: **CCR5** (R5 strains, early infection, macrophages/memory T cells) or **CXCR4** (X4 strains, later). Homozygous CCR5-Δ32 confers resistance; maraviroc blocks CCR5.

## Simplified explanation

HIV uses CD4 plus CCR5 (or CXCR4) to get into cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The best assay(s) to measure specific cytokines(s) include ...

A. Blast formation
B. T-cell proliferation
C. Measurement of leukocyte chemotaxis
D. ELISA testing
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Blast formation | **F** | Measures lymphocyte transformation, not a specific cytokine. |
| B. T-cell proliferation | **F** | A functional assay, not cytokine-specific. |
| C. Measurement of leukocyte chemotaxis | **F** | Not specific for a cytokine. |
| D. ELISA testing | **T** | Sandwich ELISA quantifies a specific cytokine. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Specific cytokines are measured by **immunoassays** (sandwich ELISA, multiplex bead arrays, ELISpot for secreting cells, intracellular cytokine flow cytometry). Bioassays (proliferation, chemotaxis) are less specific.

## Simplified explanation

ELISA uses antibodies against the exact cytokine, so it measures it specifically.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

IL-10 acts as an antagonist to ...

A. IL-4
B. TNF-α
C. IFN-γ
D. TGF-β
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IL-4 | **F** | IL-10 and IL-4 are both Th2-associated; not antagonists. |
| B. TNF-α | **T** | IL-10 suppresses macrophage production of TNF-α. |
| C. IFN-γ | **T** | IL-10 inhibits IFN-γ production and Th1 responses. |
| D. TGF-β | **F** | Both are regulatory/anti-inflammatory. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**IL-10** (from Tregs, Th2, macrophages) is anti-inflammatory: it inhibits Th1 cytokine synthesis (**IFN-γ**, IL-2), down-regulates MHC II and co-stimulators on APCs, and suppresses macrophage **TNF-α**, IL-1, IL-12 production.

## Simplified explanation

IL-10 calms inflammation by blocking IFN-γ and TNF-α.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The force of attraction between a pentavalent antibody and a single antigenic determinant is characterized by ...

A. Affinity
B. Avidity
C. Van der Waals attraction
D. Covalence
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Affinity | **T** | Affinity = strength of binding between one binding site and one epitope. |
| B. Avidity | **F** | Avidity is the total binding strength of all sites with a multivalent antigen. |
| C. Van der Waals attraction | **F** | One of the non-covalent forces contributing to affinity, not the term that characterises it. |
| D. Covalence | **F** | Antigen-antibody binding is non-covalent. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Affinity**: intrinsic strength of a single antibody-combining site for a single epitope (non-covalent: hydrogen bonds, electrostatic, van der Waals, hydrophobic). **Avidity**: overall strength of multivalent binding (e.g. pentameric IgM to a multivalent antigen), greater than the sum of affinities.

## Simplified explanation

Binding to one epitope is affinity; binding through many sites at once is avidity.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following technique(s) is/are typified by radial immunodiffusion combined with electrophoresis ...

A. Countercurrent electrophoresis
B. Rocket electrophoresis
C. Immunoelectrophoresis
D. Southern blotting
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Countercurrent electrophoresis | **F** | Antigen and antibody move towards each other (double diffusion + electrophoresis). |
| B. Rocket electrophoresis | **T** | Laurell rocket: antigen electrophoresed into antibody-containing gel (single radial diffusion + electrophoresis). |
| C. Immunoelectrophoresis | **F** | Electrophoresis followed by double diffusion. |
| D. Southern blotting | **F** | DNA hybridisation technique. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Rocket (Laurell) immunoelectrophoresis** drives antigen into agarose containing antibody; rocket height is proportional to antigen concentration (quantitative, like radial immunodiffusion). Counterimmunoelectrophoresis and immunoelectrophoresis are based on double diffusion.

## Simplified explanation

Rocket electrophoresis is radial immunodiffusion sped up with an electric field.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

When soluble antigens diffuse in a gel that contains antibody, the zone in which optimum precipitation occurs is/are ...

A. Prozone
B. Zone of equivalence
C. Postzone
D. Prezone
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prozone | **F** | Antibody excess: little precipitation. |
| B. Zone of equivalence | **T** | Optimal lattice formation. |
| C. Postzone | **F** | Antigen excess: little precipitation. |
| D. Prezone | **F** | Same as prozone (antibody excess). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Precipitin curve: **prozone** (antibody excess), **zone of equivalence** (maximal lattice and precipitation), **postzone** (antigen excess). Prozone can cause false negatives (e.g. syphilis serology), corrected by dilution.

## Simplified explanation

Maximum precipitation happens at equivalence, when antigen and antibody are balanced.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is/are primary lymphoid organ(s) ...

A. Lymph node
B. Spleen
C. Thymus
D. MALT
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Lymph node | **F** | Secondary lymphoid organ. |
| B. Spleen | **F** | Secondary lymphoid organ. |
| C. Thymus | **T** | Primary lymphoid organ (T-cell maturation). |
| D. MALT | **F** | Secondary lymphoid tissue. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primary (central)** lymphoid organs: **bone marrow** (B-cell development) and **thymus** (T-cell maturation), where lymphocytes acquire receptors and tolerance. **Secondary**: lymph nodes, spleen, MALT/tonsils, Peyer's patches, where immune responses are initiated.

## Simplified explanation

The thymus (and bone marrow) are where lymphocytes are made and educated; the others are where they meet antigen.
hint: Where lymphocytes mature vs where they work.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The type of cell(s) that would be found in a primary follicle is/are ...

A. Unstimulated B cells
B. Germinal centers
C. Plasma cells
D. Memory cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Unstimulated B cells | **T** | Primary follicles contain resting naive B cells. |
| B. Germinal centers | **F** | Germinal centres define secondary follicles. |
| C. Plasma cells | **F** | Found in medullary cords/red pulp. |
| D. Memory cells | **F** | Generated in germinal centres of secondary follicles. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primary follicles** = aggregates of resting, unstimulated (naive) B cells with follicular dendritic cells. After antigen stimulation they become **secondary follicles** with **germinal centres** (proliferation, somatic hypermutation, class switching, memory and plasma cell generation).

## Simplified explanation

Primary follicles hold resting B cells; germinal centres, plasma cells and memory cells come after stimulation.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Which of the following is/are true of NK cells?

A. They rely on memory for antigen recognition
B. They share antigens with B cells
C. They are found mainly in lymph nodes
D. They recognize a lack of MHC proteins
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. They rely on memory for antigen recognition | **F** | NK cells are innate; classically no antigen-specific memory. |
| B. They share antigens with B cells | **F** | They share markers with **T cells** (CD2, CD7). |
| C. They are found mainly in lymph nodes | **F** | Mainly in blood, spleen and liver. |
| D. They recognize a lack of MHC proteins | **T** | 'Missing self': loss of MHC class I removes inhibitory signals. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

NK cells (CD56⁺CD16⁺CD3⁻, large granular lymphocytes) kill virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation. Inhibitory receptors (KIR, CD94/NKG2A) recognise **MHC class I**; cells that lose MHC I ('missing self') are killed via perforin/granzyme. They also mediate ADCC via CD16.

## Simplified explanation

NK cells kill cells that have lost their MHC class I 'ID card'; they don't need memory.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the thymus, positive selection of immature T cells is/are based upon the recognition of which of the following ...

A. Self-antigens
B. Stress proteins
C. MHC antigens
D. µ chains
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Self-antigens | **F** | Strong self-antigen recognition causes deletion (negative selection). |
| B. Stress proteins | **F** | Not the basis of selection. |
| C. MHC antigens | **T** | Thymocytes that bind self-MHC survive (MHC restriction). |
| D. µ chains | **F** | B-cell heavy chains. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In the thymic cortex, **positive selection** keeps double-positive thymocytes whose TCR binds **self-MHC** with low/moderate affinity (MHC restriction; CD4 for class II, CD8 for class I). In the medulla, **negative selection** deletes cells that bind **self-antigen** strongly (central tolerance, AIRE).

## Simplified explanation

Positive selection keeps T cells that can recognise self MHC; negative selection removes those that react strongly to self-antigens.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Which receptor(s) on T cells is responsible for rosetting with sheep red blood cells.

A. CD2
B. CD3
C. CD4
D. CD8
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. CD2 | **T** | The E-rosette receptor (binds LFA-3 homologue on SRBC). |
| B. CD3 | **F** | TCR signalling complex. |
| C. CD4 | **F** | Co-receptor for MHC II. |
| D. CD8 | **F** | Co-receptor for MHC I. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**CD2** (LFA-2) on T cells binds CD58 (LFA-3) and its sheep homologue on sheep red cells, the basis of the historical **E-rosette** test for enumerating T cells.

## Simplified explanation

CD2 makes T cells form rosettes with sheep red cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Which of the following can be attributed to antigen-stimulated T cells.

A. Humoral response
B. Plasma cells
C. Cytokines
D. Antibody
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Humoral response | **F** | Humoral immunity is antibody (B-cell) mediated. |
| B. Plasma cells | **F** | Derived from B cells. |
| C. Cytokines | **T** | Activated T cells secrete cytokines (IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-4...). |
| D. Antibody | **F** | Produced by plasma cells. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Antigen-stimulated T cells proliferate and secrete **cytokines** (helper functions), and CD8⁺ cells become cytotoxic. Antibodies and plasma cells belong to the B-cell (humoral) arm, although T-cell help is required for most antibody responses.

## Simplified explanation

Activated T cells make cytokines; antibodies and plasma cells come from B cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the classical pathway, activation of the C3 fragment is by ...

A. C1 inhibitor
B. C3 convertase
C. C4b2a
D. C5 convertase
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. C1 inhibitor | **F** | C1-INH inactivates C1r/C1s; it does not activate C3. |
| B. C3 convertase | **T** | C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b. |
| C. C4b2a | **T** | C4b2a is the classical-pathway C3 convertase. |
| D. C5 convertase | **F** | C5 convertase (C4b2a3b) cleaves C5. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Classical pathway: antigen-antibody → C1q binding → C1r/C1s activation → C1s cleaves **C4** and **C2** → **C4b2a** (classical **C3 convertase**) cleaves C3 → C3a + C3b; C3b joins to form **C4b2a3b** (C5 convertase) → C5b-9 membrane attack complex. (Some newer texts call the larger C2 fragment C2b.)

## Simplified explanation

C3 is split by the C3 convertase, which in the classical pathway is C4b2a.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Generally, complement proteins function is ...

A. bacteria lysis
B. neutralization of viral pathogens
C. opsonization of pathogen complexes
D. parasite clearance
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. bacteria lysis | **T** | Membrane attack complex lyses Gram-negative bacteria. |
| B. neutralization of viral pathogens | **T** | Complement coats and neutralises/lyses enveloped viruses. |
| C. opsonization of pathogen complexes | **T** | C3b/iC3b opsonise for phagocytosis. |
| D. parasite clearance | **T** | Complement (esp. alternative pathway) helps kill and clear some parasites. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Complement functions: **cell lysis** (MAC), **opsonisation** (C3b, iC3b, C4b), **inflammation** (anaphylatoxins C3a, C5a; C5a chemotaxis), **clearance of immune complexes** (CR1 on red cells), **virus neutralisation**, and helping B-cell responses (C3d-CR2). These contribute to defence against bacteria, viruses and parasites.

## Simplified explanation

Complement punches holes in microbes, coats them for phagocytes, neutralises viruses and helps clear parasites.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The function of the C1q is/are ...

A. cleavage of C1r
B. cleavage of C1s
C. cleavage of C2
D. cleavage of C4
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. cleavage of C1r | **F** | C1q has no enzyme activity; binding of C1q to antibody triggers C1r auto-activation. |
| B. cleavage of C1s | **F** | Activated C1r cleaves C1s. |
| C. cleavage of C2 | **F** | C1s cleaves C2. |
| D. cleavage of C4 | **F** | C1s cleaves C4. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**C1q** is the recognition molecule: its globular heads bind the Fc regions of ≥2 IgG or one IgM (bound to antigen). This conformational change auto-activates **C1r**, which cleaves **C1s**; C1s is the serine protease that cleaves **C4 and C2**. C1q itself cleaves nothing.

## Simplified explanation

C1q only binds antibody and switches on C1r; the cutting is done by C1r and C1s. All four are false.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Proteolysis of C3 results in the release of ...

A. C2a
B. C3a
C. C4a
D. C5a
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. C2a | **F** | From C2 cleavage. |
| B. C3a | **T** | The small anaphylatoxin fragment of C3. |
| C. C4a | **F** | From C4 cleavage. |
| D. C5a | **F** | From C5 cleavage. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

C3 convertase cleaves C3 into **C3a** (released, anaphylatoxin) and **C3b** (binds surfaces, opsonin, part of C5 convertase).

## Simplified explanation

Splitting C3 gives C3a and C3b.
hint: Fragments are named after their parent.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Cytokines which modulate inflammation because they have anti-inflammatory effects include ...

A. IL-10
B. IL-6
C. TNF
D. TGF-β
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IL-10 | **T** | Inhibits macrophage and Th1 cytokine production. |
| B. IL-6 | **F** | Mainly pro-inflammatory (acute-phase response, fever). |
| C. TNF | **F** | Major pro-inflammatory cytokine. |
| D. TGF-β | **T** | Suppresses lymphocyte proliferation and inflammation; promotes repair. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Anti-inflammatory/regulatory cytokines: **IL-10, TGF-β**, IL-1Ra, IL-35, IL-37. Pro-inflammatory: IL-1, **IL-6**, **TNF-α**, IL-8, IL-12, IL-17, IFN-γ.

## Simplified explanation

IL-10 and TGF-β calm inflammation; IL-6 and TNF drive it.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The best test to perform to determine if a patient is allergic to rye grass is/are ...

A. total IgE testing.
B. skin prick test.
C. direct antigen test.
D. complement fixation.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. total IgE testing. | **F** | Total IgE is non-specific. |
| B. skin prick test. | **T** | Detects allergen-specific IgE on skin mast cells (wheal and flare). |
| C. direct antigen test. | **F** | Not an allergy test. |
| D. complement fixation. | **F** | Type I allergy does not involve complement. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Diagnosis of type I allergy to a specific allergen: **skin prick testing** or **allergen-specific IgE** (RAST/ImmunoCAP). Total IgE is raised in many conditions (atopy, parasites) and does not identify the allergen.

## Simplified explanation

A skin prick test with rye grass extract shows whether the patient has IgE against it.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Central tolerance occurs during ...

A. Lymphocyte activation
B. Lymphocyte development
C. Myeloid activation
D. Thymic selection
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Lymphocyte activation | **F** | Tolerance during activation in the periphery is peripheral tolerance. |
| B. Lymphocyte development | **T** | In primary lymphoid organs while lymphocytes mature. |
| C. Myeloid activation | **F** | Not related. |
| D. Thymic selection | **T** | Negative selection of T cells in the thymus. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Central tolerance** is established in the **thymus** (T cells) and **bone marrow** (B cells) during development: strongly self-reactive cells are deleted (negative selection), B cells may undergo receptor editing, and some T cells become Tregs. **Peripheral tolerance** (anergy, Tregs, deletion, ignorance) controls cells that escape.

## Simplified explanation

Central tolerance happens while lymphocytes are developing, e.g. thymic selection.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Immunological tolerance is/are ...

A. antibody dependent
B. antigen dependent
C. non-specific
D. specific
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. antibody dependent | **F** | Tolerance is a state of unresponsiveness, not mediated by antibody. |
| B. antigen dependent | **T** | Induced by exposure to the specific antigen. |
| C. non-specific | **F** | It is antigen-specific. |
| D. specific | **T** | Unresponsiveness to one antigen while other responses remain intact. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Tolerance is an **antigen-induced, antigen-specific** unresponsiveness of lymphocytes, as opposed to non-specific immunosuppression.

## Simplified explanation

Tolerance is triggered by a particular antigen and applies only to that antigen.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Regulatory T-cells induce immunosuppression by secreting ...

A. IL-10
B. IFN-γ
C. TGF-β
D. Macrophages
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IL-10 | **T** | Inhibitory cytokine. |
| B. IFN-γ | **F** | A Th1 effector cytokine. |
| C. TGF-β | **T** | Inhibitory cytokine. |
| D. Macrophages | **F** | Macrophages are cells, not secreted products. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

CD4⁺CD25⁺FOXP3⁺ **Tregs** suppress through **IL-10**, **TGF-β**, IL-35, CTLA-4 (removes CD80/86 from APCs), IL-2 consumption and cytolysis.

## Simplified explanation

Tregs release IL-10 and TGF-β to quieten other immune cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Possible causes of autoimmunity in man include ...

A. cytokine dysregulation
B. inappropriate MHC expression
C. modification of self-antigens
D. sequestered antigens
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. cytokine dysregulation | **T** | Imbalance of cytokines can break tolerance. |
| B. inappropriate MHC expression | **T** | Aberrant MHC class II on non-APCs presents self-antigen. |
| C. modification of self-antigens | **T** | Drugs, infection or chemicals can create neo-antigens. |
| D. sequestered antigens | **T** | Release of hidden antigens (lens, sperm) triggers responses. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Mechanisms of autoimmunity: release of **sequestered antigens**, **molecular mimicry**, **modified self-antigens**, **inappropriate MHC class II expression**, polyclonal B-cell activation, **cytokine dysregulation**, defective Tregs/apoptosis, genetic factors (HLA), hormones.

## Simplified explanation

All four can break tolerance and cause autoimmunity.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Females have a higher incidence of autoimmunity than males perhaps due to ...

A. anatomical structure
B. hormonal influences.
C. microchimerism
D. sex chromosomes
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. anatomical structure | **F** | Not a recognised explanation. |
| B. hormonal influences. | **T** | Oestrogens enhance immune responses; androgens suppress. |
| C. microchimerism | **T** | Fetal cells persisting after pregnancy may trigger autoimmunity. |
| D. sex chromosomes | **T** | X-linked immune genes, escape from X inactivation. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Female predominance (e.g. SLE ~9:1) is attributed to **sex hormones** (oestrogen promotes B-cell survival and antibody production), **X chromosome** effects (e.g. TLR7 escaping X-inactivation) and **fetal microchimerism**.

## Simplified explanation

Hormones, the X chromosome and fetal cells left after pregnancy may explain why women get more autoimmune disease.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Autoimmune conditions include ...

A. Grave's disease
B. Pernicious anaemia
C. Rheumatoid arthritis
D. Vitiligo
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Grave's disease | **T** | Stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibodies. |
| B. Pernicious anaemia | **T** | Anti-parietal cell and anti-IF antibodies. |
| C. Rheumatoid arthritis | **T** | Systemic autoimmune arthritis. |
| D. Vitiligo | **T** | Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Organ-specific: Graves' disease, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, pernicious anaemia, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, myasthenia gravis. Systemic: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's, scleroderma.

## Simplified explanation

All four are autoimmune diseases.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, agglutination tests can be used to detect ...

A. IgA
B. IgE
C. IgG
D. IgM
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IgA | **F** | IgA RF exists but is not detected by routine agglutination. |
| B. IgE | **F** | Not relevant. |
| C. IgG | **F** | IgG RF agglutinates poorly and is not what agglutination tests detect. |
| D. IgM | **T** | IgM rheumatoid factor agglutinates IgG-coated latex/sheep cells. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Rheumatoid factor** is an autoantibody against the Fc of IgG. Latex agglutination (IgG-coated latex) and Rose-Waaler (IgG-sensitised sheep red cells) tests mainly detect **IgM RF** because pentameric IgM agglutinates efficiently. Anti-CCP antibodies (ELISA) are more specific for RA.

## Simplified explanation

Agglutination tests pick up IgM rheumatoid factor.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

General characteristic(s) of hypersensitivity reaction(s) include ...

A. antibody is involved in all reactions.
B. either self-antigen or heterologous antigen may be involved.
C. immune responsiveness is depressed.
D. the antigen triggering the reaction is a harmful one.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. antibody is involved in all reactions. | **F** | Type IV is T-cell mediated. |
| B. either self-antigen or heterologous antigen may be involved. | **T** | Both foreign and self antigens can trigger hypersensitivity. |
| C. immune responsiveness is depressed. | **F** | Responsiveness is exaggerated. |
| D. the antigen triggering the reaction is a harmful one. | **F** | Usually harmless antigens (pollen, food). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hypersensitivity = exaggerated or inappropriate immune response causing tissue damage, to **foreign (often harmless)** or **self** antigens. Gell and Coombs: type I (IgE), II (IgG/IgM to cell-bound antigen), III (immune complexes), IV (T cell, delayed).

## Simplified explanation

Hypersensitivity is an over-reaction, often to harmless or self antigens, and type IV doesn't need antibody.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is/are associated with type I hypersensitivity ...

A. activation of complement.
B. an inherited tendency to respond to allergens.
C. cell-bound antibody bridged by antigen.
D. release of preformed mediators from mast cells.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. activation of complement. | **F** | Type I is IgE/mast cell mediated. |
| B. an inherited tendency to respond to allergens. | **T** | Atopy. |
| C. cell-bound antibody bridged by antigen. | **T** | Allergen cross-links IgE on FcεRI. |
| D. release of preformed mediators from mast cells. | **T** | Histamine, proteases, heparin. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Type I: sensitisation produces **IgE**, which binds FcεRI on mast cells/basophils; re-exposure **cross-links** bound IgE → degranulation (preformed **histamine**, tryptase, heparin) and synthesis of leukotrienes, prostaglandins, PAF, cytokines. **Atopy** is the genetic predisposition.

## Simplified explanation

Type I is allergy: atopy, allergen bridging IgE on mast cells and histamine release; complement isn't involved.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Secondary pharmacological agents that mediate type I hypersensitivity reactions include ...

A. Bradykinins
B. Leukotrienes
C. Prostaglandins
D. Some cytokines
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Bradykinins | **T** | Generated secondarily (kinin system). |
| B. Leukotrienes | **T** | Newly synthesised lipid mediators. |
| C. Prostaglandins | **T** | Newly synthesised lipid mediators. |
| D. Some cytokines | **T** | e.g. IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TNF. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primary** (preformed) mediators: histamine, serotonin, heparin, proteases, eosinophil/neutrophil chemotactic factors. **Secondary** (newly synthesised): **leukotrienes**, **prostaglandins**, PAF, **bradykinins**, **cytokines**.

## Simplified explanation

All four are made after activation, so they are secondary mediators.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following explains the difference(s) between type II and type III hypersensitivity reactions.

A. IgG is involved only in type III reactions.
B. Type II involves cellular antigens.
C. Type II reactions involve no antibody.
D. Type III involves IgE.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IgG is involved only in type III reactions. | **F** | IgG is involved in both. |
| B. Type II involves cellular antigens. | **T** | Type II targets cell-surface/matrix antigens; type III involves soluble antigen in immune complexes. |
| C. Type II reactions involve no antibody. | **F** | Type II is antibody mediated. |
| D. Type III involves IgE. | **F** | IgE is type I. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Type II: IgG/IgM against antigens on **cells** or tissue (transfusion reactions, HDFN, AIHA, Goodpasture). Type III: IgG/IgM + **soluble** antigen form immune complexes that deposit and activate complement (serum sickness, SLE nephritis, Arthus).

## Simplified explanation

Both use antibodies; type II hits antigens on cells, type III uses free-floating complexes.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In type II hypersensitivity reactions ...

A. antigens induce cross linking between IgE and mast cells
B. antibodies directed against cell surface antigens mediate cell destruction
C. antigen-antibody complexes are deposited in various tissues
D. antigens are directed against activated macrophages
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. antigens induce cross linking between IgE and mast cells | **F** | That is type I. |
| B. antibodies directed against cell surface antigens mediate cell destruction | **T** | Defining feature. |
| C. antigen-antibody complexes are deposited in various tissues | **F** | That is type III. |
| D. antigens are directed against activated macrophages | **F** | Describes nothing in type II (type IV involves activated macrophages). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity: IgG/IgM bind cell-surface antigens → complement lysis, opsonisation and phagocytosis, ADCC, or receptor stimulation/blocking (Graves', myasthenia gravis).

## Simplified explanation

Type II means antibodies attack antigens on cells and destroy them.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Typical manifestations of type III hypersensitivity reactions include ...

A. serum sickness
B. necrotizing vasculitis
C. rheumatoid arthritis
D. glomerulonephritis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. serum sickness | **T** | Classic systemic immune complex disease. |
| B. necrotizing vasculitis | **T** | Immune complex deposition in vessels. |
| C. rheumatoid arthritis | **T** | Immune complexes (RF-IgG) in joints. |
| D. glomerulonephritis | **T** | Immune complex deposition in glomeruli. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Type III: serum sickness, Arthus reaction, post-streptococcal **glomerulonephritis**, SLE, **vasculitis** (polyarteritis), **rheumatoid arthritis** (immune complex component), farmer's lung.

## Simplified explanation

All four are caused by immune complexes depositing in tissues.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Causes of chronic inflammation includes ...

A. obesity
B. infections
C. autoimmunity
D. tissue damage
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. obesity | **T** | Adipose tissue produces inflammatory cytokines (low-grade inflammation). |
| B. infections | **T** | Persistent infections (TB, H. pylori). |
| C. autoimmunity | **T** | Persistent self-antigen. |
| D. tissue damage | **T** | Persistent injury/foreign material. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Chronic inflammation results from persistent **infections**, prolonged exposure to toxic agents or **tissue damage**, **autoimmunity**, and metabolic/low-grade inflammation in **obesity** (adipokines, TNF, IL-6).

## Simplified explanation

All four keep inflammation going.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Indicate whether each of the following statements is true or false:

A. Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG antibodies against measles confers short-term immunity on the fetus.
B. Attenuated vaccines are more likely to induce cell-mediated immunity than killed vaccines are.
C. One disadvantage of DNA vaccines is that they don't generate significant immunologic memory.
D. Macromolecules generally contain a large number of potential epitopes.
E. A DNA vaccine only induces a response to a single epitope.
F. Hereditary retinoblastoma results from overexpression of a cellular oncogene.
G. Multiple copies of cellular oncogenes are sometimes observed in cancer cells.
H. Viral integration into the cellular genome may convert a proto-oncogene into a transforming oncogene.
I. All oncogenic retroviruses carry viral oncogenes.
J. The immune response against a virus-induced tumor protects against another tumor induced by the same virus.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG antibodies against measles confers short-term immunity on the fetus. | **T** | Natural passive immunity lasting months. |
| B. Attenuated vaccines are more likely to induce cell-mediated immunity than killed vaccines are. | **T** | Live organisms replicate intracellularly and present via MHC I. |
| C. One disadvantage of DNA vaccines is that they don't generate significant immunologic memory. | **F** | DNA vaccines do generate memory. |
| D. Macromolecules generally contain a large number of potential epitopes. | **T** | Large molecules are multi-epitope. |
| E. A DNA vaccine only induces a response to a single epitope. | **F** | The encoded protein contains many epitopes. |
| F. Hereditary retinoblastoma results from overexpression of a cellular oncogene. | **F** | It results from loss of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene. |
| G. Multiple copies of cellular oncogenes are sometimes observed in cancer cells. | **T** | Gene amplification (e.g. MYCN, HER2). |
| H. Viral integration into the cellular genome may convert a proto-oncogene into a transforming oncogene. | **T** | Insertional activation. |
| I. All oncogenic retroviruses carry viral oncogenes. | **F** | Some act by insertional mutagenesis without carrying an oncogene. |
| J. The immune response against a virus-induced tumor protects against another tumor induced by the same virus. | **T** | Virus-induced tumours share viral antigens. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T, E F, F F, G T, H T, I F, J T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Passive maternal IgG protects infants for months. Live attenuated vaccines induce both humoral and cell-mediated immunity; DNA vaccines express whole proteins (many epitopes) and induce memory. Retinoblastoma is due to loss of the **RB1 tumour suppressor** ('two hits'). Oncogene activation: point mutation, **amplification**, translocation, **retroviral insertion**. Virus-induced tumours share viral antigens, so immunity cross-protects (unlike chemically induced tumours).

## Simplified explanation

Maternal IgG and live vaccines give the immunity described; DNA vaccines do make memory and many epitopes; retinoblastoma is a lost brake (RB1), not an overactive oncogene; not all oncogenic retroviruses carry oncogenes; tumours from the same virus share antigens.

body: State any TWO (2) disadvantages of using live attenuated organisms as vaccines.
answer:
Any two:

- **Reversion to virulence** (e.g. vaccine-derived poliovirus from OPV).
- **Unsafe in immunocompromised** people and pregnancy (can cause disease).
- Need a **cold chain**: heat-labile, short shelf life.
- Risk of **contamination** with other agents during production.
- Possible **spread** to unvaccinated contacts; interference by maternal antibody.

> [!answer]
> Possible reversion to virulence and danger in immunocompromised recipients (also cold-chain requirement).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, BCG, OPV, yellow fever, varicella, rotavirus) give strong, long-lasting humoral and cell-mediated immunity, often after a single dose, but carry these safety and logistic drawbacks compared with inactivated/subunit vaccines.

## Simplified explanation

Live vaccines can occasionally become harmful again or cause disease in people with weak immunity, and they must be kept cold.

body: A young girl who had never been immunized to tetanus stepped on a rusty nail and got a deep puncture wound. The doctor cleaned out the wound and gave the child an injection of tetanus antitoxin. If the girl receives no further treatment and steps on a rusty nail again 3 years later, will she be immune to tetanus?
answer:
**No.** Tetanus antitoxin is **passive immunisation** (preformed antibody). It neutralises toxin immediately but is catabolised within weeks (IgG half-life ~3 weeks), and it does **not stimulate her own B and T cells**, so **no memory** forms. Three years later she would have no protective antibody; she needs active immunisation with **tetanus toxoid** (plus antitoxin/TIG for the new wound).

> [!answer]
> No: antitoxin gives short-lived passive immunity without memory; she needs tetanus toxoid.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Passive immunity (antitoxins, immunoglobulins, maternal IgG) is immediate but temporary; active immunity (infection or vaccination, e.g. toxoid) takes time to develop but induces memory. Tetanus infection itself does not reliably confer immunity because the toxic dose is below the immunogenic dose.

## Simplified explanation

The antitoxin only lent her antibodies for a few weeks; her body made no memory, so she isn't protected 3 years later.

body:
For each of the following descriptions, choose the most appropriate term from: *Sarcoma; Carcinoma; Metastasis; Neoplasm; Malignant; Leukemia; Transformation; Lymphoma; Benign*.

133. A benign or malignant tumor
134. A tumor that has arisen from endodermal tissue
135. A tumor that is invasive and continues to grow
136. A tumor that has arisen from lymphoid cells
137. A tumor that is noninvasive
138. A permanent change in the genome of a cell that results in abnormal growth
139. Cancer cells that have arisen from hematopoietic cells that do not grow as a solid tumor
140. A tumor that has arisen from mesodermal connective tissue
answer:
| # | Term |
|---|---|
| 133 | **Neoplasm** |
| 134 | **Carcinoma** |
| 135 | **Malignant** |
| 136 | **Lymphoma** |
| 137 | **Benign** |
| 138 | **Transformation** |
| 139 | **Leukemia** |
| 140 | **Sarcoma** |

(Metastasis, the spread of tumour cells to distant sites, is not used.)

> [!answer]
> Neoplasm, Carcinoma, Malignant, Lymphoma, Benign, Transformation, Leukemia, Sarcoma.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Carcinomas arise from endodermal or ectodermal epithelia; sarcomas from mesodermal connective tissue; leukaemias from haematopoietic cells growing as single cells in blood/marrow; lymphomas from lymphoid cells as solid tumours. Benign tumours do not invade; malignant ones invade and may metastasise. Transformation is the heritable change converting a normal cell into a cancer cell.

## Simplified explanation

Match each description: any tumour = neoplasm, epithelial = carcinoma, invasive = malignant, lymphoid = lymphoma, non-invasive = benign, genetic change = transformation, blood cancer = leukaemia, connective tissue = sarcoma.
